solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Certainly not a club competition: all theoretically may play — here?

parts.note: an open tournament is one any qualifying player may in principle enter, as with golf's Open Championship
Sandwich in Kent is home to Royal St George's, a golf course where the Open has been staged

explanation.surface: Someone muses that a golf championship anyone might enter is no club event, and wonders where it might be held.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal St George's at Sandwich, an English seaside town in Kent, hosts golf's Open Championship, so the Open at Sandwich is a real event. 'Club' means a three-decker club sandwich, not a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A single slice of bread with toppings is the opposite of a stacked, triple-layer club sandwich.

clue.text: Film showing tackle to many spectators?

definitions.meaning: a 1982 British comedy film set among an army concert party
slang 'tackle' is the genitals, so men displaying their private parts to an audience

explanation.surface: A film reviewer notes a picture in which tackle, sports gear perhaps, is displayed before a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'tackle' and 'privates' both mean the male genitals; soldiers drawn up for inspection are on parade.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a Peter Nichols play later filmed with John Cleese, about a wartime army entertainment unit.

clue.text: Fellow who's drunk 1 litre

indicators.note: something drunk is unsteady and reeling, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: the figure 1 is written out as the word one

explanation.surface: A man who has knocked back a whole litre of drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is a man's given name, and crosswords use 'fellow' to clue any male first name.

clue.text: 'Flabby' takes it in, embracing tip from doctor

definitions.text: 'Flabby' takes it in, embracing tip from doctor

indicators.note: embracing means holding something within, so the rearranged letters wrap round the doctor's letter
flabby means loose and slack, so the letters of the following words are shaken out of shape
the tip of a word is its first letter, here the start of doctor

explanation.surface: An overweight patient adopts a regime after taking a hint from their GP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flabby' is both the anagram signal and the reason for the diet: read whole, the clue describes a plump person taking up a doctor-suggested eating plan.
explanation.definitionFit: The low-carbohydrate eating plan devised by Dr Robert Atkins is something a flabby person might adopt on medical advice.

clue.text: Disciplinary fellow grips the writer lower

indicators.note: grips means holds tightly, so the college officer's word closes round the writer's

parts.note: a dean is the college fellow responsible for discipline
the writer is the setter speaking of themselves, giving me

explanation.surface: A strict college official takes hold of the author, perhaps to humiliate them.
explanation.definitionFit: To degrade or debase someone's dignity is to lower them; both are verbs.

clue.text: Fashionable Miss Hunter Jones, intrepid adventurer

parts.note: something fashionable is in
Diana is the Roman goddess of the hunt, a maiden huntress

explanation.surface: A stylish young woman named Hunter, surnamed Jones, is described as a daring explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss Hunter' looks like a woman's surname; it is the virgin huntress-goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana Jones is the whip-cracking archaeologist hero of the Spielberg films, an intrepid adventurer surnamed Jones.

clue.text: One cherishing street criminal in secret

parts.note: one who hugs, holding something close and dear, is a hugger
a mugger robs people in the street

explanation.surface: Someone who loves a thug who robs passers-by keeps it quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: The old phrase means secrecy or confusion, and is used adverbially for doing things covertly.

clue.text: Gorgeous East European's taken in on the way to London

indicators.note: taken in means received inside, so the Balkan national holds the travel word

parts.note: a Serb is a native of Serbia; the 's is 'is'
travelling to the capital is going up to London, so up

explanation.surface: A handsome traveller from Serbia is welcomed aboard on the journey to the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage one goes 'up' to London from anywhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb and gorgeous are both strong adjectives of praise meaning magnificent.

clue.text: Beginners to find unsafe jags in mountain

indicators.note: beginners are the opening letters, taken here from each of the four following words

explanation.surface: Novice climbers discover dangerous sharp rocks on a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: Fuji is Japan's highest peak, the volcanic cone near Tokyo.

clue.text: Goes out without novel that's in red woolly drawer?

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the jumbled letters sit round the next pieces
out here means disordered or wrong, so the letters of goes are put out of place

parts.note: Kim is Rudyard Kipling's novel
OD stands for overdrawn, the state of an account in the red

explanation.surface: Someone goes out without a book, apparently into a red woolly drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawer' is something that draws, i.e. pulls a sled, not a piece of furniture; 'without' is the old word for outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A husky-type sled dog hauls sledges and has a thick coat, making it a shaggy puller of loads.

clue.text: Pill, say, purser must take

indicators.note: say signals that the words are to be spoken, so a phrase heard the same is wanted

parts.note: a ship's purser allocates the cabins, so must take charge of the berths

explanation.surface: A ship's officer is told to take a tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' is not an example marker for 'Pill' but the sound signal: berth control, a purser's job of managing cabins, is pronounced like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The oral contraceptive is commonly called the pill, the best-known form of contraception.

clue.text: Twisted cinema killer and jewel thief

indicators.note: twisted means wrung out of shape, so the letters of cinema are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warped picture-house becomes the haunt of a murderer and gem robber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ice' is slang for diamonds, so a jewel thief can be so called; the name was also the nickname of contract killer Richard Kuklinski.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang term covers both a cold-blooded hit man and a diamond robber, ice being underworld slang for gems.

clue.text: See 2
In Rule 10, note offence to revolutionise game

indicators.note: In sits before the pieces it is placed into, so the note goes within the rule and number

parts.note: a law is a rule
10 is ten

indicators.note: to revolutionise is to turn round, so the word for offence is read backwards

parts.note: a sin is an offence

explanation.surface: A sports regulation, number ten, cites an offence that will transform play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' at the start looks like scene-setting, but it is the container signal for the note.
explanation.definitionFit: The racket sport played on grass courts, as at Wimbledon, is one particular game.

clue.text: Following charge, see lake antelope on plateaux

indicators.note: Following tells us the lake and antelope pieces come after the charge

parts.note: a tab is a bill or charge, as in a bar tab
L is the map abbreviation for lake
elands are large African antelope; antelope can be plural

explanation.surface: After paying, a safari tourist spots antelope by a lake on high flat ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised areas of fairly level land are both plateaux and these, a plural for a plural.

clue.text: Healing ointment used in tribal medicine

indicators.note: used in says the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A soothing salve forms part of a tribe's traditional remedies.
explanation.definitionFit: A soothing salve rubbed on to heal or comfort is a balm.

clue.text: See 19
Theatrical pitching place

definitions.meaning: a site where tents are pitched

explanation.surface: A dramatic venue for throwing a ball, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: flamboyantly showy behaviour, and a site for tents.

clue.text: Wicked explosive second batch at 6 o'clock's gone off

parts.note: mo is a moment, a second, as in 'half a mo'
a lot is a batch, as at auction

indicators.note: gone off means exploded or gone wrong, so the letters here are scrambled

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral six
the letters of o'clock; the 's is 'has'

explanation.surface: A wicked bomb, the second lot of them, detonated at six.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' means having a wick, not evil; the petrol bomb is lit by a rag fuse.
explanation.definitionFit: A petrol bomb is a bottle bomb lit by a rag fuse, so it literally carries a wick.

clue.text: Inappropriate income revised — and covered by criminal bung

indicators.note: covered by means enclosed, so the reworked income sits inside the other letters
criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters of bung are twisted
revised means altered, so the letters of income are reordered

explanation.surface: Improper earnings are adjusted and hidden by a crooked bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bung' is British slang for a bribe, which makes the surface about corruption; here it is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbecoming conduct is unsuitable or unseemly, so the two adjectives share a meaning.

clue.text: Like working actor — out of touch?

definitions.meaning: an employed actor is appearing in a stage production
in rugby or football a ball brought back from touch, the area beyond the sideline, is live again

explanation.surface: A busy performer seems disconnected from reality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touch' is the area off the side of a rugby or football pitch; a ball out of it is live.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: performing in a drama, and a ball live on the pitch rather than off it.

clue.text: Not just public entertainment, visiting Madame La Guillotine?

indicators.note: a trip to the guillotine costs one's head, so the leading letter is lopped off

parts.note: a funfair is a public entertainment of rides and stalls

explanation.surface: A show for the people is hardly fair when the guillotine is in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing F, the first letter, from FUNFAIR gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unjust or inequitable is not fair, so not just.

clue.text: Deceased — or not? With the same dimensions!

definitions.meaning: one who has died is spoken of as no more with us; the query admits it may just mean 'not any more'
of equal length, so not exceeding the other in length

explanation.surface: Is someone dead or not? They are the same size, anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase into 'no' plus the comparative of 'long'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'not any more', used of the dead, and literally 'not of greater length'.

clue.text: European capital's low hills — panoramic?

indicators.note: a panoramic photo is made by swinging round from one spot, so the last letter swings round to the start

parts.note: kopjes are small hills of the South African veld, a word from Afrikaans

explanation.surface: A city noted for its low hills offers a sweeping view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'panoramic?' moves the S of KOPJES to the front. A kopje is a small hill on the South African veld.
explanation.definitionFit: Skopje is the capital city of North Macedonia, in the Balkans.

clue.text: The notion of hide-and-seek?

indicators.note: of signals the letters are taken out of the game's name

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the point of a children's hiding game is.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit in 'hIDE-And'; the hyphen is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a thought or concept, the same as an idea.

clue.text: With skill updated loco in a rush

indicators.note: in places the locomotive word inside the plant word

parts.note: a rush is a reed, a waterside plant
a loco, short for locomotive, gives train

explanation.surface: An engine driver hurries through refresher training.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loco' and 'rush' look like speed words; they are a locomotive and a marsh plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone retrained has been taught again, giving them refreshed and modern abilities.

clue.text: Mountains out of time, sadly

indicators.note: out of means without, so the time letter leaves the range's name

parts.note: the Atlas Mountains are a range in north-west Africa

explanation.surface: Climbers lament that they have run out of time on the peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection expresses sorrow or regret, used like 'unfortunately' or 'sadly'.

clue.text: Equine establishment in position, so turn left

indicators.note: in puts the following pieces inside the word for position

parts.note: the lie of something is its position, as in the lie of the land or of a golf ball
so, as in 'so good', means very
a turn or go is a stab, as in 'have a stab at it'

explanation.surface: A rider at a riding school is told to hold position, then turn left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word but is the container signal; 'turn' means a go or attempt, not a change of direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A livery stable keeps and feeds horses for their owners for payment, or hires them out.
